title: Build the inference engine state machine
subtitle: Correct ownership is the foundation of high throughput.
outcomes: Represent request progress independently from physical batch slots.
Implement page ownership and admission invariants.
Use randomized traces to validate completion, preemption, and reclamation.
body:
## A batch is temporary; a request has a life

A model forward pass consumes tensors and returns tensors. A serving engine manages computations that arrive, pause, grow, finish, or disappear while those tensors are in flight. The difficult abstraction is persistent request identity. A request may occupy batch row three now and row zero next iteration. Its token history, cache mapping, random-number state, output position, and lifecycle must survive that movement.

Start with an explicit request object: identifier, arrival time, prompt tokens, number of computed prompt tokens, generated tokens, logical KV length, page table, sampling state, deadline, and lifecycle status. Separate “tokens known to the host” from “tokens whose KV has been computed.” The newest sampled token often exists before its own KV is computed on the next decode invocation. Conflating these counts produces subtle cache-length errors.

A minimal lifecycle might be queued, prefilling, decoding, retiring, and terminal. Terminal outcomes include completed, cancelled, failed, and rejected. Retiring means no new work should be scheduled but some in-flight work still owns buffers. A single `done` boolean cannot express that distinction cleanly.

## Make one iteration a transaction

An engine iteration selects runnable work, reserves any required pages, constructs tensor inputs and metadata, launches execution, and commits results after completion. The scheduler should not partially mutate a request and then discover that it cannot allocate the remaining pages. Either preflight all reservations or provide a precise rollback path.

The selected batch is a view of request state, not its owner. Maintain a mapping from each physical row to request ID and logical token positions. When a request finishes, compacting the next batch should move this mapping alongside every associated tensor. Output tokens, lengths, and sampling state must all be associated by the same identity. A row-number bug can produce fluent text belonging to the wrong request, which ordinary “output looks reasonable” tests will miss.

```python
# Conceptual iteration contract; actual device execution may be asynchronous.
plan = scheduler.choose(requests, token_budget, free_pages)
reservation = cache.reserve(plan)
try:
    result = executor.run(plan, reservation)
    commit_by_request_id(plan, result)
except Exception:
    retire_or_rollback(plan, reservation)
```

The exception path must distinguish work that never launched from work that may still be executing. Rolling back logical state does not magically stop a device write. This is why retirement belongs in the design before performance optimizations.

## Pages turn sequence growth into local allocation

For page size $P$, logical token index $t$ maps to logical page $\lfloor t/P\rfloor$ and offset $t\bmod P$. The request's block table maps that logical page to a physical page. Attention follows the table while preserving logical order. The allocator need only provide another page when the valid length crosses a boundary.

Take a pool of eight pages holding four tokens each. Requests of lengths five, eight, and three occupy two, two, and one pages: five pages total. Appending one token to each requires no new page for the five-token request, a new page for the eight-token request, and no new page for the three-token request. Reservation must inspect lengths, not simply assume every active request costs a page per iteration.

The [PagedAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) motivates this separation between logical sequence state and physical storage. Your educational engine should implement the invariant directly instead of imitating a production allocator's entire feature set. Begin without sharing, then add it only after private-page ownership is correct.

## Admission needs a policy, not an optimistic guess

Allocating only current KV maximizes immediate admission but risks exhausting memory during continued generation. Reserving every request's maximum allowed output length is conservative but can waste capacity. A middle path uses incremental allocation plus an explicit policy for pressure: pause admission, preempt selected requests, evict reusable prefixes, or recompute state later. Each choice affects latency and fairness.

Recomputation is not free, and preemption can create feedback: memory pressure causes recomputation, recomputation consumes GPU time, slower completion retains memory longer, and pressure worsens. Measure preemptions and recomputed tokens per successful request. An engine that reports high GPU utilization while repeatedly redoing work may deliver little useful progress.

Choose a simple first policy: reserve enough pages for the next planned iteration, admit only when that reservation succeeds, and reject requests whose declared maximum context cannot be supported under your stated limits. Then improve the policy experimentally. The point is to make pressure behavior observable and deterministic before making it clever.

## Build a reference execution model

Run each request independently through the tiny decoder with fixed inputs and controlled randomness. Then run the same requests through the batching engine. For greedy decoding, compare per-request logits and output tokens within the chosen numerical contract. For stochastic decoding, isolate random-number streams by request and generation position so unrelated arrivals do not silently change which draws a request receives.

A batch-shape change can still alter floating-point results and therefore sampling decisions. Separate that numerical issue from an indexing or state-ownership bug. First test a deterministic toy executor whose next output encodes request ID and token position. It should survive arbitrary compaction, cancellation, and arrival order exactly. Only after the scheduler passes that test should you integrate GPU numerics.

Read [vLLM's source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) by tracing one request from admission to completion at a pinned commit. Record the functions that own scheduling, cache allocation, execution, and output processing. Do the same later for SGLang; the useful comparison is the placement of responsibilities and invariants, not a contest over which codebase looks familiar.

The supplied scheduler script demonstrates mixed prefill/decode interference only; the allocator, admission policy, executor, and lifecycle above are the learner project. Your deliverable is an engine whose state can be inspected after every event. Generate seeded random traces with arrivals, short and long prompts, cancellations, and page-boundary crossings. Assert that every request reaches one terminal outcome, no token is delivered twice, no live page is freed, and all unretained pages return. Throughput comes next. Without these properties, faster execution merely creates corrupted state more efficiently.

exercises.title: Reserve only the pages actually needed
exercises.prompt: Pages hold four tokens. Active request KV lengths are [4,7,8,9], and each will compute one new token. How many additional pages are required, assuming their current allocations are minimal?
exercises.hint: Compare ceil(S/4) and ceil((S+1)/4) for each S.
exercises.solution: Length 4 needs one new page; 7 needs none; 8 needs one; 9 needs none. Two additional pages are needed. The old allocation is 1+2+2+3=8 pages; the new allocation is 2+2+3+3=10 pages.

exercises.title: Find a compaction corruption
exercises.prompt: Batch rows initially correspond to A, B, C. B finishes, and the next batch contains A, C. A developer compacts token inputs but leaves per-row lengths and RNG states unchanged. Design a test and explain the failure.
exercises.hint: Use requests with different lengths and deterministic distinguishable outputs.
exercises.solution: Give B and C different context lengths and use a toy executor that returns request ID plus logical position. After compaction, C receives B’s stale metadata, causing wrong masking, position, or random draws. Assert row-to-request identity for every input, length, output, and RNG handle. Compact via a single index permutation applied to all coupled state, or rebuild metadata from request objects each step.

exercises.title: Specify retirement under cancellation
exercises.prompt: A client cancels after a GPU batch launches but before it completes. Define the state transition, page-release point, and output-delivery behavior.
exercises.hint: Cancellation changes demand immediately but does not undo launched work.
exercises.solution: Mark the request retiring and exclude it from future plans. Suppress subsequent client delivery, while retaining pages and output buffers until the in-flight completion event is observed. Then decrement owners and move to cancelled terminal state. Test cancellation before launch, during execution, and immediately after completion; each must yield one terminal outcome and no use-after-free.

quiz.question: Which identity should own persistent cache and sampling state?
options: Current physical batch row.
The request ID and its logical progress.
The latest kernel launch number only.
The client socket’s buffer offset.
quiz.explanation: A request keeps its logical history while the next batch may move it to a different physical row. Storing persistent state by row alone can attach another request’s cache, length, or random draws after compaction.

quiz.question: Why distinguish sampled-token count from computed-KV length?
options: Sampling consumes no time.
KV always has twice as many tokens.
A token may be sampled before its KV is computed in the next forward step.
Generated tokens never enter the cache.
quiz.explanation: The final processed position yields logits from which the next token is sampled; that sampled token’s own KV is usually computed on the following forward step. Treating known-token count as computed-cache length can expose an uninitialized cache slot or use an incorrect position.

quiz.question: An engine runs out of pages halfway through constructing a batch. What design property prevents inconsistent state?
options: Ignoring the failed request.
Preflight reservation or a complete rollback/retirement protocol.
Increasing sampling temperature.
Reusing a random live page.
quiz.explanation: Planning and allocation must either reserve everything needed before committing or undo every partial mutation consistently. If device work already launched, rollback also needs a retirement protocol because changing host metadata does not stop an in-flight write.

quiz.question: Why can preemption reduce useful throughput despite high GPU utilization?
options: GPU utilization directly measures completed requests.
Preempted requests always disappear.
All preemption is free.
The GPU may spend time recomputing state instead of advancing requests.
quiz.explanation: GPU utilization measures activity, including recomputing KV that a prior preemption discarded. Useful throughput counts forward progress toward delivered requests, so repeated recomputation can keep the GPU busy while completion rate deteriorates.

quiz.question: What is the best first executor for stress-testing scheduler identities?
options: A large sampled language model judged by fluency.
A network endpoint with unknown retries.
A deterministic toy that encodes request identity and logical position.
An executor that emits the same token for every request.
quiz.explanation: A toy executor that encodes request ID and logical position makes swapped rows or stale metadata produce an exact, recognizable mismatch. A fluent sampled language-model answer can conceal the same ownership bug behind plausible text and numerical variation.

title: Continuous batching and chunked prefill
subtitle: Choose who advances at each iteration.

body:
## Stop making short requests wait for long ones

A static batch begins together and remains coupled until the chosen boundary. If one sequence finishes early while another generates a long answer, a rigid implementation can leave useful capacity idle or keep padding finished rows. Continuous batching changes membership at iteration boundaries: completed requests leave, runnable requests continue, and new work enters when resource budgets permit. It converts serving from a sequence of fixed groups into a repeated scheduling decision.

The word continuous does not mean every request runs continuously. At each iteration, the engine chooses which token computations advance. One request may receive a decode step; another may receive a prompt chunk; a third may wait. The scheduler must preserve causal state while deciding how to spend compute, cache capacity, and latency slack. Those resources are not interchangeable.

## A token budget is a useful approximation

Let an iteration process $n_d$ decode tokens and prompt chunks of lengths $c_1,\ldots,c_k$. A simple token budget is

$$n_d+\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_i\leq T_{max}.$$

This budget constrains the number of new token rows, which is closely related to projection work. It does not fully constrain attention work: a new token attending to a long history can cost more than one attending to a short history. It also does not guarantee KV allocation succeeds. A practical planner checks both work and memory, and an advanced planner may use an empirical iteration-time model.

Start with a decode-prioritized policy. Give active decode requests one step, then spend remaining token budget on prompt chunks. This protects token cadence under moderate load. Under persistent decode saturation, however, new prefills can starve. Add a waiting-time or deadline mechanism, and measure it. A policy is not fair merely because it is easy to describe.

## Why splitting a prompt helps another user

Consider a deliberately invented iteration model: active decode work costs 4 ms, and adding $c$ prefill tokens adds $0.01c$ ms. Processing a 4096-token prompt at once makes that iteration 44.96 ms. Every ongoing decode request in the batch experiences that long interval. Splitting the prompt into eight 512-token chunks makes each mixed iteration 9.12 ms. The new prompt now completes after 72.96 ms, but existing requests avoid the 44.96-ms interruption.

These numbers are a teaching model, not GPU measurements. They show the tradeoff cleanly: chunking protects other requests while adding repeated iteration cost and potentially reducing GEMM efficiency. On actual hardware, mixed work can amortize weight traffic, share kernels, and interact nonlinearly. Fit the real cost surface instead of assuming that prefill and decode times always add.

[Sarathi-Serve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310) is the primary reading for chunked-prefill scheduling. Reproduce the principle with a small system before trying to reproduce a paper's absolute throughput. Workload distributions, hardware, model implementation, and SLO definitions are part of the result.

## Chunking must preserve the original model

A prompt chunk beginning at logical position $a$ must attend to all permitted cached history plus its own causally preceding tokens. Its positional offsets start at $a$, not zero. Finishing a chunk does not finish the prompt unless all prompt tokens have been processed. Sampling from intermediate chunk logits as if the prompt were complete changes the request.

Build a numerical test comparing unchunked prefill with chunk sizes one, an odd number, and the whole prompt. Compare the final prompt logits and resulting KV state. Then insert decode steps for other requests between chunks and repeat. Scheduling interleaving should not contaminate one request with another's state. This test connects the scheduler to the decoder's mathematical contract.

The scheduler also needs a progress invariant. Every admitted request should either advance under the policy, wait with an observable reason, or move to a terminal state. A waiting request with no recorded reason is how starvation becomes invisible in dashboards. Track wait age and class-specific latency, especially for long prompts, short prompts, and requests with warm prefixes.

## Choose chunk sizes from evidence

Small chunks increase scheduling flexibility and may reduce worst interruptions, but introduce more iterations, metadata construction, and potentially less efficient matrix operations. Large chunks improve arithmetic utilization but consume larger latency intervals. The best value depends on the current decode population, history lengths, device, and SLO. A single global chunk size is an understandable baseline, not a universal optimum.

An adaptive policy can choose the largest chunk predicted to fit an iteration-time budget. Its prediction error matters: underestimation violates cadence, while overestimation wastes useful capacity. Measure the model's error by workload region and keep a conservative fallback. Training a sophisticated predictor on one convenient trace is less valuable than a simple policy with transparent behavior across several traces.

## Evaluate both sides of the bargain

Use the supplied discrete-event lab as a controlled environment. It provides prefill-first and chunked policies with deterministic arrivals and token timestamps, but no KV admission or static-batch implementation. Add the static baseline and admission constraints, then replay the same seeded trace across policies and chunk sizes. Keep prompt lengths, output lengths, termination policy, and cache capacity fixed. Report TTFT for new requests, inter-token gaps for active requests, completed output tokens, useful goodput, waiting time by class, and memory pressure events.

```python
# Conceptual policy; reserve pages before committing the plan.
plan = one_decode_step_for_eligible_requests()
remaining = token_budget - plan.new_token_count
plan += choose_prefill_chunks(waiting_requests, remaining, fairness_state)
```

Finally repeat a bounded subset on a real engine. A simulation demonstrates policy consequences under its assumed costs; hardware validates whether those costs and interactions are plausible. The week's deliverable should include a counterexample where your preferred policy loses. If you cannot find one, you probably have not stressed the relevant workload. Scheduling expertise means knowing which objective a decision improves, who pays for it, and when the decision should change.

quiz.question: What is the central scheduling unit in continuous batching?
options: The entire lifetime of a fixed batch.
An iteration’s selected token computations.
A checkpoint file.
A whole data center.

quiz.question: Why does a token budget fail to fully predict iteration time?

Token budgets count only network bytes.

quiz.question: Chunked prefill begins at position 100. Which positional convention preserves normal causal semantics?

quiz.question: A smaller prefill chunk improves decode ITL but worsens TTFT. How should this be reported?

As a tradeoff under a declared workload and SLO, including useful throughput.
As proof the measurement is broken.
By omitting TTFT.

title: Prefix reuse, cancellation, and CUDA graphs
subtitle: Make reusable work immutable, identifiable, and safe to retire.
outcomes: Define cache identity from the actual model computation.
Implement reference-counted prefix reuse and cancellation retirement.
Explain when graph replay saves overhead and when bucketing wastes work.
body:
## A prefix hit is a claim about computation

Two requests can share cached state only if the reused portion would have produced the same state under the same computation. Matching text is not sufficient: tokenization, model revision, adapters, positional conventions, and multimodal inputs can change the result. Matching token IDs is stronger, but still insufficient if the weights or relevant execution semantics differ. A cache key is therefore a compact statement of computational identity.

For a block-based cache, a useful conceptual key contains the parent-prefix identity, the current block's tokens, and a namespace describing model and adapter state. Parent identity matters because the KV for a token depends on preceding context. Identical token blocks appearing after different histories do not generally have identical KV. The [vLLM prefix-caching design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/) is a concrete source to study after deriving this requirement.

In multimodal requests, include a reliable identity for the embedded image, audio, or other input and its preprocessing configuration. A placeholder token saying “image here” does not identify the pixels. Likewise, a cache should not survive a weight update unless its namespace changes or its contents are invalidated. The fastest wrong reuse is still wrong.

## Reuse saves prefix work, not all future work

Suppose a 4096-token prompt shares 3584 tokens with a retained prefix and uses 16-token pages. The shared prefix consists of 224 full pages; 512 prompt tokens remain to be computed. This can substantially reduce prompt processing. Later decode queries still attend to the relevant history under full attention, so a prefix hit does not imply zero cache reads during generation.

Measure hit rate in more than one way. Request hit rate counts any reuse; token hit rate counts the fraction of prompt tokens reused; avoided-compute estimates may weight tokens by their attention context. A workload where every request hits one short block can have a high request hit rate and little saved work. Report first-token latency and retained memory alongside hit rate so reuse has an observable benefit and cost.

[SGLang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104) makes prefix reuse a central runtime concern through RadixAttention. The transferable idea is to exploit shared computation while preserving ownership and eviction rules. You need not reproduce a full radix tree to test that idea; immutable block keys and a simple retention policy are enough for a first implementation.

## Sharing and eviction have different ownership rules

Distinguish an active reference from a retention reference. Active requests need the state for correctness. A completed request may leave state retained only because future requests might reuse it. Under pressure, retained but inactive entries are eviction candidates. Active entries are not freely evictable unless the engine supports an explicit recomputation or offload protocol.

Reference counts alone do not tell you reuse value. Recency, frequency, prefix length, regeneration cost, and page pressure can inform policy. Start with LRU among evictable entries and measure it against a no-retention baseline. Cache pollution appears when a stream of one-off prompts displaces frequently reused prefixes. A more complex policy earns its place only if it improves useful throughput on representative traces without excessive bookkeeping.

Cancellation adds a second time axis: the client stops wanting output before device work necessarily stops using memory. Mark the request inactive for future scheduling immediately, suppress further delivery, and release active references only after its last in-flight operation completes. Then decide whether eligible prefix pages should remain retained. Cancellation and eviction are separate events; tying them together carelessly can either leak memory or destroy useful reuse.

## Graph replay trades dynamism for stable execution structure

CUDA graph capture records a compatible sequence of GPU operations for later replay, reducing repeated host-side submission overhead. In common framework usage, replay relies on stable storage and execution structure; input values can change through buffers prepared for the captured path. Exact restrictions depend on the APIs and implementation. Read the [PyTorch CUDA graph notes](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html) before implementing a concrete capture path.

Dynamic serving complicates reuse because batch size, cache tables, and sequence metadata change. One strategy captures a set of batch-size buckets and pads active requests to a supported bucket. With buckets 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, an active batch of nine uses the 16 bucket. Seven rows are inactive. If cost scaled linearly with rows, that would add about 78% row work relative to nine; actual decode cost often has shared weight traffic, so latency need not scale by that percentage.

Padding must be semantically inert. Dummy rows must not allocate live pages, advance request counters, consume another request's random draws, or emit output. A graph replay that is numerically correct for real rows can still corrupt engine state through dummy-row side effects.

## Compare saved overhead with introduced cost

A simple decision model is

$$\Delta T=T_{dispatch\ saved}-T_{padding}-T_{metadata}-T_{extra\ synchronization}.$$

A positive value favors graph replay under the model. Capture cost and persistent graph memory matter too, especially for short-lived workers or many buckets. Measure cold start separately from warm steady state. Graphs are most compelling when submission overhead is material; they cannot eliminate inherently expensive attention or communication.

This week's learner extension combines three mechanisms deliberately: reusable immutable prefix pages, cancellation-aware retirement, and a simulated graph-bucket planner. The supplied scheduler isolates scheduling interference; prefix caching, ownership, cancellation, and graph planning are all new learner work. Actual GPU graph capture is also not implemented by that script. Test cache namespace changes, partial-page divergence, cancellation at every lifecycle stage, and dummy rows. Then implement actual graph replay only on supported hardware and compare identical requests with capture disabled. A polished performance optimization has a clear identity contract, a release protocol, and a measured regime where its extra complexity pays for itself.

exercises.hint: The shared prefix is stored once; each suffix remains private.
exercises.solution: Without sharing: 10×1280=12,800 token states. With sharing: 1024+10×256=3584. Savings are 9216 token states, or 72% of the original payload. Compute savings also depend on which request populated the cache and whether the prefix was already retained.

exercises.title: Find the graph-bucket break-even point
exercises.prompt: An eager batch of nine spends 80 microseconds on dispatch and 400 on GPU work. A bucket-16 replay spends 15 on dispatch, 450 on GPU work, and 10 on metadata updates. Ignore capture amortization. Is replay faster?
exercises.hint: Compare complete times, not only launch overhead.
exercises.solution: Eager totals 480 microseconds. Replay totals 475, so the gain is only 5 microseconds or about 1.011×. The 65-microsecond dispatch saving is mostly consumed by 50 more GPU microseconds and 10 metadata microseconds. Capture cost, persistent memory, or measurement noise could reverse this tiny advantage.

quiz.question: Why must a block-cache key depend on the parent prefix?
options: Parent keys reduce the number of model layers.
Physical pages always have the same ID.
Token IDs are globally unique sentences.
The same token block can produce different KV after different preceding context.
quiz.explanation: The hidden state and KV for a token depend on preceding context, so equal local token blocks can represent different computations. Chaining the parent-prefix identity distinguishes those histories; local token bytes alone cannot justify reuse.

quiz.question: What does a prefix hit usually avoid?
options: All future attention reads.
All sampling.
All output-token projections.
Recomputing the matching prefix state.
quiz.explanation: A hit avoids recomputing the matching prefix’s state during prompt processing. New generated tokens still run through the model and, for full attention, read relevant cached history, so a prefix hit does not make subsequent decode free.

quiz.question: Which retained cache entry can a simple eviction policy reclaim safely?
options: Any entry with many tokens.
One with no active or in-flight owners, subject to its retention policy.
Any entry after the client sees the first token.
Every entry from a cancelled request before GPU completion.
quiz.explanation: An inactive retained entry can be reclaimed only after all active references and asynchronous readers or writers have finished. A client disconnect is not enough: its last launched kernel may still require the page even though no further output will be delivered.

quiz.question: Which dummy-row behavior breaks graph-bucket correctness?
options: Using an explicitly masked output.
Not delivering a dummy token.
Advancing a real request’s RNG or cache counters.
Keeping dummy metadata separate.
quiz.explanation: Padding rows are execution scaffolding and must have no effect on live request state. Advancing a real request’s RNG, length, or cache counters changes later results even if the padded row’s immediate output is discarded.

quiz.question: What most strongly supports adding CUDA graphs?
options: A high prefix hit rate alone.
A large checkpoint file.
A measured host submission bottleneck with replay savings exceeding padding and management costs.
A claim that graphs eliminate attention FLOPs.
quiz.explanation: Graph replay is justified when measured submission savings exceed padding, metadata updates, extra synchronization, and amortized capture cost. A large model or a high cache-hit rate alone says nothing about that balance; profile the actual host and GPU critical path.

title: Reliable serving is part of performance
subtitle: An engine is useful only when it handles overload, cancellation, and failure.
outcomes: Design bounded admission, deadlines, and explicit terminal outcomes.
Instrument request progress from client arrival to delivered output.
Evaluate recovery and overload without concealing failed or censored work.
body:
## The useful unit is a completed promise

A token emitted by a GPU is not necessarily a token delivered to a user. Tokenization, queueing, model execution, detokenization, buffering, networking, and client consumption lie along the path. A slow consumer can accumulate output buffers even when the GPU is fast. A disconnected client can leave expensive generation running. A retry can duplicate work. A high-performance service must define what it promises and where that promise ends.

Begin with a request contract: model revision, input limits, output limit, timeout or deadline, streaming behavior, and terminal outcomes. Define whether the deadline includes queueing and network delivery. For a client-facing SLO it usually must include the relevant user-visible path. Keep internal execution timing as a separate diagnostic, not a substitute for the service metric.

Each request should reach exactly one recorded terminal outcome. Completion means its defined output finished successfully. Cancellation, rejection, timeout, and execution failure are distinct outcomes because they have different causes and remedies. A benchmark that simply discards all non-completions is measuring the easy survivors.

## Bound queues before they become hidden memory

If arrival work exceeds service capacity for long enough, a queue grows without bound unless the system rejects, delays upstream, or reduces work. More buffering cannot create compute capacity. It can absorb a short burst, but beyond that it converts overload into latency and memory pressure. Bound admission by estimated work and state requirements, not only request count: one 100,000-token prompt is not equivalent to one 20-token prompt.

A useful first policy has limits for queued requests, queued prompt tokens, active KV pages, and maximum wait age. It rejects work that cannot reasonably meet the declared contract, while recording the reason. A deadline-aware policy may estimate remaining queue delay plus service time, but its estimator must be tested for underprediction. The [Google SRE overload chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/) supplies general operational principles; the inference-specific resource model comes from your own measurements.

Consider a replica capable of 100 units of work per second. A burst supplies 180 units/s for five seconds, after which load returns to 60. If no work is dropped and the capacity remains constant, the queue accumulates $(180-100)\times5=400$ units. At the subsequent net drain rate of 40 units/s, clearing it takes ten seconds. A five-second burst can therefore affect users for much longer than five seconds. If retries increase arrival work, recovery can take longer still.

## Retries are new demand

In a toy independent-failure model with failure probability $p$ per attempt and unlimited retry, expected attempts per successful request are $1/(1-p)$. At $p=0.2$, that is 1.25 attempts: 25% extra demand. Real overload failures are correlated with load, so retries can amplify the condition causing them. Use bounded retries, backoff, jitter, and a deadline budget when those semantics fit the application. Do not retry blindly after streaming partial output without defining how the client should interpret the new attempt.

Idempotency needs precise scope. A request identifier can help a server recognize a repeated submission, but it does not automatically ensure exactly-once token delivery across reconnects. Streaming events need stable sequence positions if a client may resume or deduplicate them. A restarted worker may have lost its KV state. The service must either reconstruct it under a declared policy or report that the stream cannot continue seamlessly.

## Backpressure must reach the expensive work

If a client reads slowly, an unbounded server-side output queue becomes a memory leak in practice even when every buffer has an eventual owner. Put a bound on buffered output, then choose whether to pause generation, disconnect the slow consumer, or spool under a documented limit. Pausing one request should not block unrelated requests through a global lock or shared queue.

Cancellation should propagate from network layer to scheduler to cache retirement. Measure cancellation-to-stop-scheduling time and cancellation-to-resource-release time separately. The latter includes legitimate in-flight work. A server that acknowledges cancellation immediately while generating the entire answer anyway has poor useful efficiency even if its happy-path throughput looks excellent.

## Instrument causes, not only symptoms

For each request, record timestamps at arrival, queue admission, prefill start/end, token readiness, token delivery, and terminal outcome where available. Use one monotonic clock within a process. Across machines, separate clock-offset uncertainty from actual latency or use trace spans whose boundaries are meaningful without naive timestamp subtraction.

Aggregate queue depth, wait age, active sequences, free KV pages, retained prefix pages, preemptions, recomputed tokens, batch sizes, and output-buffer occupancy. A jump in TTFT could come from queueing, cold prefixes, tokenization, or prefill execution. The counters should distinguish those possibilities. Avoid using request IDs as high-cardinality metric labels; preserve detailed identifiers in bounded traces or logs instead.

```python
# Every offered request must land in exactly one final accounting bucket.
assert offered == completed + rejected + cancelled + timed_out + failed + outstanding
```

At the end of a drained experiment, outstanding should be zero or explicitly censored. Track retry attempts separately from user requests so the accounting does not confuse extra work with additional successful demand.

## Test the failure path while the system is busy

The supplied scheduler currently completes synthetic requests without admission limits or failure handling. Extend it with injected execution errors, slow consumers, cancellation, and bursts. Then test a real service with bounded fault injection: terminate a worker, force a timeout, disconnect a client, and fill the admission queue. Verify page recovery and exactly one terminal record per request. Measure recovery time and the effect on unrelated requests.

Your report should show goodput under the same quality and latency contract before, during, and after a fault. Include failed requests and retry work in the denominator appropriate to the metric. Separate engine-only speed from delivered-service performance. The exit standard is not that every request succeeds under arbitrary overload; that is impossible with finite resources. It is that the system fails predictably, preserves state integrity, recovers resources, and makes its limitations visible.

## Optional Berkeley application checkoff

The [Spring 2026 Assignment 4 download](https://scalable-ai.eecs.berkeley.edu/S2026/assets/assignment_4.zip) is titled *Applications*. Its requirements connect backend selection to a usable interface, quality evaluation, system measurements, and a working demonstration. Use it as an external review checklist after implementing your server. For this course, choose the model and hardware justified by your experiment; the Berkeley handout’s allowed-checkpoint rules belong to that assignment. Your original extension is the scheduler dashboard and failure-injection study in Project 01. Publish your own evidence and credit the external brief.

exercises.prompt: A service handles 80 work units/s. Arrivals are 140 units/s for four seconds, then 50 units/s. With no rejection, compute backlog and ideal drain time after the burst.
exercises.hint: Accumulation and drain use different net rates.
exercises.solution: Backlog is (140−80)×4=240 units. After the burst, net drain is 80−50=30 units/s, so drain time is eight seconds. Total affected period can extend at least twelve seconds from burst start, and actual latency depends on scheduling and per-request work.

exercises.title: Account for every offered request

exercises.hint: Terminal outcomes must be disjoint, and attempts are not user requests.
exercises.solution: Fifteen user requests remain outstanding or unaccounted for because listed outcomes sum to 985. Report them as outstanding/censored until resolved; do not exclude them. The 100 retries increase attempt count to 1100 if each is an additional attempt, but user demand remains 1000. Track attempt failures and request terminal outcomes separately to avoid double counting.

exercises.title: Design slow-consumer isolation
exercises.prompt: Specify a bounded streaming-buffer policy and a test showing one stalled client cannot exhaust memory or stall every request.
exercises.hint: Backpressure must affect the corresponding generation request.
exercises.solution: Set a per-request buffer limit and a maximum stall duration. On reaching the limit, pause that request if supported or cancel it with an explicit outcome; preserve bounded bookkeeping. Run one nonreading client alongside several normal clients, verify total buffered bytes stay bounded, normal-client latency remains within the chosen tolerance, and the stalled request’s pages are eventually reclaimed after in-flight work retires.

quiz.question: What does a longer queue accomplish during sustained overload?
options: It increases GPU compute capacity.
It can hide overload by converting it into wait time and memory use.
It guarantees lower p99.
It removes the need for admission control.
quiz.explanation: A queue can absorb a finite burst, but sustained arrivals above capacity make backlog keep growing. Extra queue space then buys longer waits and more retained state rather than more compute throughput, so bounded admission and explicit outcomes remain necessary.

quiz.question: A client disconnects but its GPU work continues to completion. Which metric exposes the waste?
options: Cancellation-to-stop and resource-release latency, plus wasted generated work.
Only GPU utilization.
Only checkpoint size.
Only successful-request median latency.
quiz.explanation: Measure how quickly cancellation stops new scheduling and how quickly already launched work retires and releases pages. Also count abandoned generated tokens: high GPU utilization can otherwise conceal work no client still wants.

quiz.question: Why should retries be counted separately from user requests?
options: They consume additional work without necessarily representing new demand.
They always use zero GPU time.
They can never fail.
They remove the original request from history.
quiz.explanation: One user request may create multiple attempts, each consuming resources while contributing at most one user-level success. For example, 100 retries on 1000 original requests mean 1100 attempts, not 1100 independent successful demands; keep both populations visible.

quiz.question: What is wrong with reporting p99 only for requests that finished before the benchmark stopped?
options: Nothing; slow requests are irrelevant.
It censors the slowest work and can make overload appear healthy.
It necessarily overstates latency.
It includes too many samples.
quiz.explanation: An overloaded run tends to leave its slowest requests unfinished, so dropping them biases the reported tail toward the faster survivors. Drain the run under a stated timeout or retain unfinished requests as censored outcomes alongside latency results.

quiz.question: Which observation most directly supports slow-client isolation?
options: One stalled stream causes all token delivery to pause.
Total buffered memory grows indefinitely.
Per-request buffers stay bounded while normal clients retain their declared service quality.
The GPU remains busy regardless of output demand.
quiz.explanation: The intended property is that one client’s inability to consume output has bounded memory and scheduling consequences. Normal clients must continue meeting the stated service contract while the slow request is paused or terminated and its resources are eventually recovered.

## More GPUs introduce a new critical path

Splitting a model can reduce per-device weight storage and arithmetic. It also creates dependencies across devices. A result that was local becomes a message, and the next operation may wait for it. The right question is not “Which parallelism flag should I use?” It is “Which tensor lives where, and which operation needs information from elsewhere?” Draw those ownership boundaries before launching a cluster.

Data parallel inference replicates the model and sends different requests to different replicas. It can improve aggregate capacity when a model fits on one device, but does not automatically speed up one request. Tensor parallelism partitions operations inside layers. Pipeline parallelism partitions layers into stages. Context parallelism partitions sequence-related work. Expert parallelism partitions MoE experts. These dimensions can be combined, but each adds a placement and communication problem.

## Derive a collective from a linear layer

For $Y=XW$, partition $W$ by output columns: $W=[W_0,W_1]$. Each rank computes $Y_i=XW_i$, which is a different slice of the output. If the next operation can consume that partition directly, no immediate gather is necessary. If it needs full $Y$, an all-gather can assemble the slices. Communication depends on the next consumer, not merely on the current matrix multiply.

Now partition $W$ by input rows and partition $X$ compatibly. Each rank computes a partial contribution $Z_i=X_iW_i$ to the same output coordinates. The complete output is $Y=\sum_i Z_i$, requiring a reduction. An all-reduce gives every rank the sum; a reduce-scatter gives each rank a shard of that sum when the next operation can remain sharded. This distinction determines both bytes and downstream layout.

The [Megatron-LM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053) is a foundational example of arranging layer partitions to avoid unnecessary communication. Its subject is training, so derive the inference forward path explicitly rather than copying backward-pass costs into a serving model.

## Know what each primitive promises

All-reduce combines corresponding values and makes the result available to all ranks. All-gather concatenates rank-owned pieces in a defined rank order. Reduce-scatter reduces corresponding values and distributes output shards. All-to-all sends different pieces to different destinations, which is central to expert token routing. A collective is a data-layout contract, not just a synchronization point.

Read the [NCCL collective semantics](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/collectives.html) and test tiny distinguishable tensors first. For example, rank zero contributes $[1,2]$ and rank one contributes $[10,20]$. Sum all-reduce should yield $[11,22]$ on both. All-gather should preserve rank ordering rather than add values. This elementary test catches surprisingly expensive misunderstandings before they become multi-GPU model bugs.

All participants must follow compatible collective ordering and arguments. A rank taking an error branch while others enter a collective can leave the group waiting. Timeouts, failure propagation, and restart scope belong in the runtime design. Adding a barrier everywhere may hide a race while destroying useful overlap; express the actual dependencies instead.

## Build an alpha-bandwidth model

For an illustrative ring all-reduce with $p$ ranks and $n$ bytes per rank's full input, a common simplified model is

$$T\approx2(p-1)\alpha+\frac{2(p-1)}{p}\frac{n}{B},$$

where $\alpha$ is per-step startup latency and $B$ is effective per-link transfer bandwidth under this model. Actual libraries may choose different algorithms and protocols depending on message size and topology. The equation is a reasoning tool, not a claim that NCCL always uses a ring.

With four ranks, $\alpha=5$ microseconds, $B=50$ decimal GB/s, and $n=16$ MiB, the startup term is 30 microseconds and transfer term approximately 503.3 microseconds. Total is approximately 0.533 ms. At 16 KiB, the transfer term is only about 0.492 microseconds, leaving a total near 30.49 microseconds. Small messages are dominated by repeated startup; large messages expose bandwidth.

If an architecture requires two such nonoverlapped collectives per layer across 32 layers, the small-message estimate totals about 1.95 ms per forward step. That can be substantial for latency-sensitive decode. Reducing arithmetic by a factor of four does not reduce this startup term by four. A strong scaling curve eventually flattens or reverses as local work shrinks relative to communication.

## Topology is part of the algorithm

An eight-GPU node is not a uniform abstract device. Links may differ, GPUs may share switches, and crossing nodes adds network and software costs. Effective bandwidth depends on the path, simultaneous traffic, message size, and placement. A vendor aggregate bandwidth number cannot be substituted directly for every rank-to-rank transfer.

Measure your topology with a collective size sweep using [nccl-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests), then measure the application's real communication pattern. Separate latency, algorithm bandwidth, and bus bandwidth according to the tool's definitions. Record rank placement, device interconnect, and node layout. A microbenchmark without concurrent compute may overestimate usable application bandwidth when communication and computation compete for resources.

## Choose a strategy by its losing case

If a model fits on one GPU and requests are independent, compare two replicas against a two-way tensor-parallel replica under the same total GPU budget. Replication may deliver more aggregate goodput; splitting may reduce a single request's latency or enable larger memory capacity. Neither dominates universally. Pipeline parallelism can have bubbles at small concurrency, while expert parallelism can suffer from skew and many small messages.

Use the supplied MoE routing simulator to understand ownership and traffic, then extend it with an alpha-bandwidth cost model. This is a CPU reasoning lab; actual distributed validation requires two or more compatible GPUs. Build a minimal distributed linear layer, compare its output with a single-device reference, sweep message sizes, and measure strong scaling. Your deliverable is a placement decision with evidence, including one workload where adding GPUs makes the chosen metric worse. That is the beginning of cluster-level inference judgment.

exercises.title: Derive two linear-layer partitions
exercises.prompt: For X=[M,K] and W=[K,N], describe output ownership and required communication when W is partitioned by N versus by K. Assume the next consumer needs full Y on every rank.
exercises.hint: Column partition produces disjoint outputs; row partition produces partial sums.
exercises.solution: Partition by N: each rank holds W_i=[K,N/p] and computes Y_i=[M,N/p], so all-gather reconstructs full Y. Partition by K: each rank holds X_i=[M,K/p] and W_i=[K/p,N], computes Z_i=[M,N], and all-reduce sums the contributions. If the next consumer accepts shards, communication can be delayed or changed, which is why whole-block layout matters.

exercises.title: Compute a communication floor
exercises.prompt: Use p=4, alpha=5 microseconds, B=50 GB/s, and n=1 MiB in the illustrative ring model. Then calculate 64 sequential collectives.
exercises.hint: Use 1 MiB=1,048,576 bytes and retain both startup and transfer.
exercises.solution: Startup is 30 microseconds. Transfer is 1.5×1,048,576/(50×10^9) seconds=31.45728 microseconds. Total is 61.45728 microseconds; 64 sequential collectives cost about 3.9333 ms. Overlap, another algorithm, and actual topology can change measured time, so this remains a model prediction.

exercises.title: Compare replication with tensor parallelism
exercises.prompt: A model fits on one GPU. Design an experiment comparing two single-GPU replicas with one two-GPU tensor-parallel replica under equal hardware and request traces.
exercises.hint: Measure both low-load latency and saturation goodput; routing and cache affinity can matter.
exercises.solution: Use the same checkpoint, precision, quality settings, prompt/output trace, and total two-GPU budget. Measure single-request latency at low load, then open-loop goodput/TTFT/ITL/rejections across offered rates. Record routing, prefix reuse, and total resident memory. Report GPU-seconds per completed useful request. The winner can differ between latency and aggregate capacity; do not collapse them into one unqualified speedup.

quiz.question: Column-partitioning W in Y=XW produces what on each rank?
options: A disjoint slice of output columns.
The same complete output with different random noise.
A scalar loss only.
A full output requiring summation with every other rank.
quiz.explanation: Partitioning W by output columns assigns different coordinates of Y to each rank: rank i computes XW_i. Reconstructing full Y concatenates those slices in the correct order; summing them would combine unrelated output coordinates.

quiz.question: What does reduce-scatter provide?
options: A broadcast of one rank’s original buffer.
A concatenation of all unmodified buffers.
A reduced result divided into rank-owned shards.
A guarantee of zero communication.
quiz.explanation: Reduce-scatter first combines corresponding input values across ranks, then leaves each rank with a different shard of the combined result. It is useful when the next operation can remain sharded; an all-gather would concatenate values without performing that reduction.

quiz.question: Why can tensor parallelism hurt tiny-batch decode?
options: The model stops using matrices.
Collective startup and synchronization can dominate the reduced local work.
Every GPU receives less memory bandwidth.
It always doubles model quality.
quiz.explanation: Partitioning reduces arithmetic and weight storage per device but introduces or preserves cross-device dependencies. With tiny messages and little local work, repeated collective startup and synchronization can cost more than the compute time saved.

quiz.question: Which comparison isolates the benefit of model splitting when a model fits on one GPU?
options: One two-GPU split replica versus two single-GPU replicas under the same total GPU budget and trace.
A two-GPU run versus an unrelated CPU model.
Two different precision settings on different workloads.
Peak interconnect bandwidth versus tokenizer speed.
quiz.explanation: Two independent replicas are an alternative use of the same two GPUs when the model fits on one. Compare both low-load request latency and saturation goodput on an unchanged trace, because splitting may help one objective while replication helps the other.

quiz.question: What does the ring alpha-bandwidth equation establish?
options: The exact algorithm chosen by every NCCL release.
That all-reduce has no startup cost.
A simplified cost prediction whose topology and algorithm assumptions must be checked.
That more ranks always reduce latency.
quiz.explanation: The equation predicts the startup and transfer cost of an illustrative ring under stated effective-bandwidth assumptions. NCCL can choose other algorithms or protocols, and real topology or contention changes effective cost; use the formula to generate a testable prediction, not to replace a measurement.
